title: LRU
subtitle: Data structures behind O(1) Least Recently Used eviction, LFU vs W-TinyLFU, and Redis approximated LRU.
keyTakeaways: Textbook O(1) LRU pairs a Hash Map for O(1) key lookups with a Doubly Linked List for O(1) node promotion and tail eviction.
Pure LRU is vulnerable to Scan Pollution (a one-off batch scan flushing out genuinely hot keys); frequency-aware policies like LFU and W-TinyLFU prevent this.
Production in-memory stores like Redis do not use linked lists due to memory pointer overhead, choosing probabilistic sampling across random keys instead.

sections.heading: The Mechanics of O(1) LRU and Multi-Threaded Contention
sections.body: In code interviews, an LRU cache is simply a Hash Map plus a Doubly Linked List. On every read or write, the node is spliced to the head (Most Recently Used). When memory fills up, the tail node (Least Recently Used) is evicted. In production multi-threaded systems, however, updating pointers on every read turns every cache lookup into a write, serializing concurrent readers behind a mutex.
bullets: Concurrency Bottleneck: Because reading an item modifies linked-list pointers, naive synchronization creates severe lock contention across CPU cores. Production caches (like Java Caffeine or Go Ristretto) use lock-free ring buffers to queue read events and update eviction lists asynchronously.

Scan Pollution: If your cache holds 10,000 items and a user or batch job runs a table scan over 10,000 cold records, every hot key in memory gets evicted. A single scan flushes your active working set.

Frequency Defense (LFU & W-TinyLFU): Window TinyLFU tracks frequency via a compact probabilistic Count-Min Sketch. New cold items enter a probationary admission window and are only admitted to the main cache if their historical frequency exceeds the eviction candidate's score.

sections.heading: How Redis Implements Approximated Eviction
sections.body: Storing two 64-bit pointers (`prev` and `next`) per key across 100 million keys in Redis would waste 1.6 GB of RAM purely on linked-list metadata. Redis eliminates pointer overhead by approximating LRU and LFU through probabilistic sampling.
bullets: Approximated LRU Sampling: Redis embeds a 24-bit timestamp inside each key's internal object header. When memory reaches `maxmemory`, it samples a small random pool of keys (configured via `maxmemory-samples`, default 5) and evicts the key with the oldest idle time.
allkeys-lru vs volatile-lru: `allkeys-lru` evicts any key when memory fills up; `volatile-lru` restricts eviction to keys configured with an explicit TTL, preserving unexpired persistent state.

Redis LFU (Logarithmic Morris Counter): Redis repurposes those 24 header bits to track an 8-bit logarithmic counter with continuous decay over time, providing frequency-weighted eviction that resists batch scan pollution.

tradeOffs.pros: Simple to implement; quickly adapts to shifts in temporal recency (e.g. breaking news).
tradeOffs.cons: Vulnerable to cache pollution when batch queries or crawlers read through cold data.
tradeOffs.bestFor: User session stores, ephemeral request caches, and recency-dominated feeds.

tradeOffs.pros: Resistant to scan pollution; retains high-frequency items even when cold records are read.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires periodic frequency decay tuning to ensure historical hot items don't stay trapped in memory forever.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Product catalogs, CDN edge nodes, and Zipfian/power-law traffic distributions.

interviewTip: Be ready to implement an O(1) LRU cache with a Map and Doubly Linked List, but stand out by explaining why high-throughput production systems avoid linked-list locks using asynchronous ring buffers or Redis probabilistic sampling.
